title: NEET Biology: Zoology and Human Physiology

questions.q: The enzyme that begins protein digestion in the stomach is:
questions.solution:
**Pepsin**, secreted as inactive pepsinogen and activated by the stomach's hydrochloric acid.

It works best at about **pH 2**, which is why the stomach is so acidic. Trypsin continues the job in the alkaline small intestine.

questions.q: Most absorption of digested food occurs in the:
questions.solution:
The **ileum**, whose villi and microvilli give an enormous surface area — some $250$ m$^{2}$ in all.

Each villus is one cell thick with a rich blood supply and a lacteal for fats. The large intestine absorbs water, not food.

questions.q: The blood vessel carrying oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart is the:
questions.solution:
The **pulmonary vein** — the one vein carrying **oxygenated** blood.

The pulmonary artery is its mirror exception. Arteries and veins are defined by direction relative to the heart, not by what they carry.

questions.q: The normal human haemoglobin content is about:
questions.solution:
About **12–16 g/dL** — somewhat higher in men than women.

Below this range is **anaemia**, usually from iron deficiency, and the symptoms are tiredness and breathlessness because oxygen delivery falls.

questions.q: Gaseous exchange in humans takes place in the:
questions.solution:
The **alveoli** — about 300 million of them, giving some $80$ m$^{2}$ of surface, walls one cell thick, moist and richly supplied with capillaries.

Every feature answers a requirement for fast diffusion.

questions.q: The functional unit of the kidney is the:
questions.solution:
The **nephron** — about a million per kidney.

Filtration at the glomerulus, then **selective reabsorption** along the tubule recovers nearly everything: of $180$ litres filtered daily, only $1$–$2$ litres leaves as urine.

questions.q: The part of the brain that controls balance and coordination is the:
questions.solution:
The **cerebellum**.

The cerebrum handles thought and voluntary action; the **medulla** controls heartbeat, breathing and blood pressure; the **hypothalamus** regulates temperature, hunger, thirst and the pituitary.

questions.q: Which gland is called the master gland?
questions.solution:
The **pituitary**, which secretes hormones controlling the thyroid, adrenals and gonads as well as growth.

It is itself directed by the **hypothalamus**, so the true master is arguably the brain.

questions.q: Fertilisation in humans normally occurs in the:
questions.solution:
In the **ampulla of the fallopian tube**.

The zygote then divides as it travels down and implants in the uterine wall about a week later.

questions.q: A cross between two heterozygous individuals gives a phenotypic ratio of:
questions.solution:
$\text{Tt} \times \text{Tt}$ gives **3 : 1** by phenotype and $1:2:1$ by genotype.

The $9:3:3:1$ ratio belongs to a **dihybrid** cross, and it is just $3:1$ happening twice independently.

Uracil replaces thymine in **RNA**. The complementary pairing is what makes accurate replication possible — each strand is a template for the other.

questions.q: The number of codons that code for amino acids is:
questions.solution:
There are $4^{3} = 64$ codons in all, of which **3 are stop codons**, leaving $\mathbf{61}$ that specify amino acids.

Since there are only 20 amino acids, the code is **degenerate** — most amino acids have several codons, which buffers the effect of point mutations.

questions.q: The theory of natural selection was proposed by:
questions.solution:
**Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace**, who presented it jointly in 1858.

Lamarck's rival idea was the inheritance of **acquired** characteristics, which Weismann's mouse-tail experiment disproved. De Vries contributed the mutation theory.

T lymphocytes handle cell-mediated immunity. Memory cells are what make **vaccination** work, giving a rapid response on a second exposure.
